tier_label: Hard case: the obvious diagnosis is wrong
title: Catch Them If You Can

briefing.headline: Plagiarism and assessment in higher education: what you should know before the call
points: A Flemish university college (hogeschool) with professional bachelor programmes; lecturers both teach and assess.

Students can copy-paste from websites in seconds, and paid essay-writing websites ('essay mills') sell custom papers. Commercial plagiarism-detection software compares submitted work against the internet and a database of papers; how reliable its scores are is debated.
Assessment rules (exam regulations) are set at institution level and changed through formal governance once a year.
Accusing a student of fraud triggers a formal procedure with appeal rights.

stakeholder.name: Prof. Ilse Verbruggen
stakeholder.voice: Thoughtful, academic, a little tired. Weighs her words, likes nuance, quotes a study occasionally. Protective of both lecturers and students. Allergic to hype in either direction.

frontline.name: Sarah Aerts
frontline.role: Lecturer in business management, ten years in
frontline.voice: Sharp, funny, overworked. Has opinions about committees. Cares about students, including the ones who cheat.

opening_message: Plagiarism. Fraud cases are exploding and the exam board is drowning. We bought detection software last year, but using it is optional, so I'd like it made compulsory for every take-home paper, plus an academic-honesty module on the learning platform that all 9,000 students complete before the second semester. The exam board would also like tougher sanctions, but that is their department. Can you help us set this up?
surface_ask: Compulsory detection-software checks on every paper plus an academic-honesty e-learning module for all 9,000 students (and, if the exam board gets its way, tougher sanctions).

gold.real_problem: The fraud cases are not spread across the college: 71% come from 31 course units in three business programmes, almost all taught by part-time lecturers from the field appointed in the last four years. They inherited generic, single-submission take-home essays that can be copy-pasted together or bought from an essay mill, and nobody ever taught them how to design an assignment that can't be, or how to run a short oral authenticity check. The usual suspects are already in place and not working: the regulations have allowed an oral authenticity conversation since 2006 (used nine times), the detection software has been running all year with its settings fixed in September, sanctions were tightened last year and students already sign an honesty statement. Where lecturers use staged drafts, personal or local briefs and oral checks (nursing, IT), cases are near zero and the few cases that do arise hold up on appeal.
gold.need_statement: About 45 part-time lecturers teaching the 31 most affected course units in Business Management, Communication Management and Office Management need to be able to redesign their own assignments so they can't simply be copied or bought (staged drafts, briefs tied to the student's own internship or a local case, in-class components) and to run a fair ten-minute oral authenticity check under the existing art. 41bis. Train them hands-on, with the nursing and IT pioneers, before the second semester. More detection, more rules, tougher sanctions or a student e-learning module would treat a skill gap as a discipline problem, and training all 600 lecturers would bury the 45 who need it.

hidden_facts.fact: 151 of the 212 fraud cases (71%) come from 31 course units in Business Management, Communication Management and Office Management; 27 of those 31 units are taught by part-time lecturers from the field appointed in the last four years. Units with staged drafts or an oral component produced 4 cases between them.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks where the cases come from: which programmes, courses or lecturers, or for a breakdown of the case data.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: I've only ever seen the total. Let me ask the exam board secretary for the breakdown... Oh. Thirty-one course units. That is not 'exploding'. That is a neighbourhood.
hidden_facts.data_doc: 212 suspected plagiarism cases, academic year to date. By programme: Business Management 74, Communication Management 49, Office Management 28, all other 19 programmes 61. The 151 cases in the three business programmes come from 31 course units; 27 of these are taught by part-time lecturers appointed 2003-2007. Assessment format of all units with cases: single final take-home submission 192 cases; staged drafts or oral component 4 cases; other 16.
hidden_facts.data_source: Lecturer contracts joined with the exam board case register

hidden_facts.fact: 61% of fraud cases are dismissed on appeal, mostly because a similarity score is not evidence and bought papers match nothing. Of the 83 upheld cases, 64 had draft versions or a record of an oral conversation on file.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks how fraud cases end, what the exam board sees, or what makes a case hold up.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: 129 of 212 didn't survive appeal. The ones that did mostly had drafts or a conversation on file. 'The software says 43%' does not impress the ombudsperson. Or me, frankly.
hidden_facts.data_doc: 212 cases. Upheld: 83. Dismissed or overturned on appeal: 129 (61%). Main reasons for dismissal: similarity report only, no other evidence (71); flagged passages correctly referenced (22); suspected purchased paper, no match found (31); other (5). Upheld cases with drafts or a recorded oral conversation on file: 64 of 83.
hidden_facts.data_source: Exam board report, academic year to date

hidden_facts.fact: Since September 2006, art. 41bis of the exam regulations lets any lecturer hold a short oral 'authenticity conversation' about any written assignment, without announcing it in the course sheet. It has been used nine times in a year by 600 lecturers.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks what the rules already allow, whether lecturers may check authenticity orally, or whether a policy change is needed.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Ah. Yes. Art. 41bis. I chaired that working group. Lecturers may ask any student to explain their paper, no notice needed. It's been used nine times. Nine. I've had more fire drills.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Art. 41bis (in force since 1 September 2006): for any written assignment, the examiner may invite the student to a short oral conversation to verify authorship. Prior mention in the course sheet is not required. Recorded uses, academic year 2006-2007: 9 (Nursing 5, Applied IT 3, Business Management 1).
hidden_facts.data_source: Exam regulations, art. 41bis, and exam board log

hidden_facts.fact: The detection software (Naspeur) has run on every uploaded paper since last year. After the student council showed second-language writers were flagged three times as often, ICT changed the settings in September to exclude quotes and reference lists; the gap closed, but cases kept rising.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks about the detection software: how it is used, how reliable or fair it is, or whether making it compulsory would help.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: The software isn't the issue, it already checks almost everything uploaded. There was an unpleasant analysis about second-language students; ICT fixed the settings in September. The flags got fairer. The cases didn't go down.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Naspeur similarity checks, academic year to date: 11,840 papers checked (94% of take-home submissions uploaded to the learning platform). Settings changed 15 September: quotes and reference lists excluded. Flag rate above 25% before/after: first-language writers 9% / 7%; second-language writers 27% / 8%. Suspected purchased papers with a match found: 0.

hidden_facts.fact: Sanctions were already tightened last year (zero for the whole course unit instead of the assignment) and every student signs an honesty statement with each submission since 2005. Cases rose 40% anyway.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks what the college has already tried against plagiarism: sanctions, policy, student awareness.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Tougher sanctions? We did that last year. And the students sign an honesty declaration with every paper. They sign it very honestly.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Plagiarism policy, revised June 2006: proven plagiarism leads to zero for the whole course unit (previously: the assignment). Honesty statement mandatory on every submission since 2005. Suspected cases: 2005-2006: 151; 2006-2007 to date: 212.
hidden_facts.data_source: Plagiarism policy and exam board annual figures

hidden_facts.fact: The basic teaching qualification for new lecturers covers lecturing, rubrics and grading, but nothing on designing assessments or checking authorship. Part-timers inherit the course sheet and the assignment from their predecessor and often ask colleagues how to write an assignment that can't be bought.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks how new or part-time lecturers learn to design assessments, what training they've had, or who wrote the assignments in the affected courses.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: New lecturers do the basic teaching qualification. It covers... lecturing. And grading. Designing an assignment? I suppose we assumed that came with the job.
hidden_facts.frontline_line: The part-timers come to me every semester. Lovely people, real experience, they run marketing departments. They got last year's essay question in a folder and a login. One asked me, very sincerely, how you write an assignment that a website can't sell. Nobody ever showed them.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Basic teaching qualification (BKO), 6 sessions: 1 Lecturing large groups; 2 Activating teaching methods; 3 Using the learning platform; 4 Rubrics and grading; 5 Feedback; 6 Student guidance. Assessment design: not included. Participation of part-time lecturers appointed 2003-2007: 41 of 52.
hidden_facts.data_source: Educational development unit, BKO programme and attendance

hidden_facts.fact: Two part-timers tried an authenticity conversation after a suspicious paper; with no idea what to ask, they asked general questions, the student coped, and both cases collapsed. They won't try again.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks the frontline whether lecturers ever check authorship themselves, or what happens when they suspect a bought paper.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: I believe one or two tried the oral conversation. I don't know how it went.
hidden_facts.frontline_line: Two of the part-timers tried the oral thing. Asked 'so, tell me about your paper'. The kid had read it on the train, did fine, case closed. You have to ask about choices, drafts, the bit they cut. Nobody told them that. Now they say orals don't work.

hidden_facts.fact: Lecturers in nursing and IT redesigned their assessments after a two-afternoon workshop from the educational development unit in 2005: staged drafts, briefs tied to the student's own internship, short oral checks. They have almost no cases, and the ones they have hold up.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks whether anyone is already doing it differently, or about good practice inside the college.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Nursing and IT. They did a workshop with our educational developers two years ago and changed everything. Drafts, internship-based assignments, short orals. Hardly any cases. Hardly any noise either.
hidden_facts.frontline_line: Nursing and IT went through a redesign workshop in 2005. Drafts, a ten-minute oral, assignments about your own internship that no essay website can sell you. They barely have cases. Nobody asked them to show the business programmes.

hidden_facts.fact: About 70% of course assessments are take-home written work across the college, in nursing and IT as much as elsewhere; the difference is design. In the three business programmes, 81% of take-home units are a single generic final essay unchanged for three years or more.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks how students are assessed, what kind of assignments are affected, or about assessment design.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Most of our assessment is take-home writing, everywhere. Nursing too. But in the business programmes it's often one final essay, same topic as last year, and the year before. Efficient. It was.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Take-home written work as main assessment: all programmes 70%; Nursing 72%; Applied IT 68%; Business, Communication and Office Management 74%. Of take-home units with drafts or an oral component: Nursing 85%, Applied IT 77%, the three business programmes 9%. Single final essay unchanged for three years or more: business programmes 81%, college average 48%.

volunteered_facts: Fraud cases have 'exploded' and the exam board is overloaded.
The college already bought detection software last year; she thinks it should simply be compulsory.
She sees it as a matter of student honesty and enforcement, not of teaching.

constraints.budget: Professional development budget of about 30,000 euro; lecturer time, especially part-timer time, is the scarce resource.
constraints.deadline: Second semester in February; course sheets for next academic year are due in May.
constraints.audience: 600 lecturers across 22 programmes; about 45 part-time lecturers teach the most affected course units. Part-timers have jobs in the field and are paid per teaching hour.
constraints.schedule: Teaching loads are high; professional development happens on two 'education days' a year, which many part-timers can't attend.
data_available: Fraud case register with course unit and lecturer
Exam regulations and exam board log
data_not_available: Any reliable measure of how many students actually buy papers from essay websites

dependencies.concern: Overloaded and convinced the answer is tougher sanctions and compulsory detection.
dependencies.if_ignored: They keep pushing enforcement and treat redesign as going soft.

dependencies.who: Programme heads of Business, Communication and Office Management
dependencies.concern: Own the course units, teaching assignments and the part-timers' hours.
dependencies.if_ignored: The part-timers never get released for the workshop and nothing changes in the 31 units.

dependencies.concern: Part-timers are paid per teaching hour; development time isn't in their contract.
dependencies.if_ignored: The people who need it most can't come, or come unpaid and resentful.

dependencies.concern: Two people who ran the 2005 workshop for nursing and IT; capacity is limited.
dependencies.if_ignored: No one to run it, or it becomes a lecture instead of hands-on redesign.

dependencies.concern: Will object to treating all 9,000 students as suspects and still remembers the flagging analysis.
dependencies.if_ignored: A fight about compulsory detection that distracts from the real fix.

dependencies.concern: Compulsory upload of every paper to the vendor's database abroad is a question under the 1992 privacy law.
dependencies.if_ignored: Making detection compulsory could become the scandal.

traps: Completion rate of the student honesty e-learning.
Share of papers run through the detection software.
Number of fraud cases detected: going up looks like success.
Number of lecturers 'trained', counted across all 600.

gold_plan.baseline: Cases and appeal outcomes per course unit; assessment design of the 31 affected units (single submission, unchanged for years); art. 41bis uses per programme.
gold_plan.behaviour: The targeted part-timers hand in a redesigned assignment for the second semester (drafts, personal or local brief, in-class part) and run authenticity conversations with a question guide when they suspect fraud.
gold_plan.leading_indicators: Number of the 31 units with a redesigned assignment by February; art. 41bis uses and their outcomes; course sheets changed for next year by May.
gold_plan.business_metric: Suspected cases in the 31 units, share of cases upheld on appeal, and exam board workload.
gold_plan.collection: Exam board case register by course unit, art. 41bis log, course sheet audit, short check-in with the part-timers after the first semester round.

concepts.conventional: Make detection compulsory, roll out an academic-honesty e-learning to all 9,000 students, and toughen sanctions.
concepts.solid: A hands-on assessment redesign workshop (two afternoons or evenings, paid) for the roughly 45 part-time lecturers teaching the 31 most affected units, run by the educational development unit with the nursing and IT pioneers: each lecturer brings their own assignment and leaves with a redesigned one (staged drafts, internship or local-case brief, in-class part) ready for February, plus practice running a ten-minute authenticity conversation under art. 41bis with a question guide. No regulation change, no new software, no student e-learning needed.
next_level_examples: Pair each part-timer with a nursing or IT pioneer for one semester: one redesign, one co-held oral check.
Rehearse authenticity conversations with student council volunteers playing the suspect, so lecturers learn which questions expose a bought paper.

Build a small library of 'unbuyable' assignment patterns from the pioneers and add an assessment-design session to the basic teaching qualification so the next intake of part-timers doesn't need rescuing.
also_valid: A one-page guide on reading similarity reports, as a side note to the redesign workshop.
Starting with the ten units with the most cases if not all 45 can be released before February.
red_flags: Saying this isn't a training problem and recommending policy or regulation changes that already exist.
Making detection compulsory or buying more software.
A student honesty e-learning or tougher sanctions as the main response.
Training all 600 lecturers in the same thing.
Detector training as the main response.

defence_objections: Only the part-timers in three programmes? The other 555 will feel accused of nothing and the 45 will feel accused of everything.
They're paid per teaching hour and run companies in the daytime. You want two afternoons from them before February?
And the exam board? They want sanctions. If I come back with 'a workshop', they'll say we've gone soft.
question_you_didnt_ask: Which courses do the fraud cases actually come from, and who teaches them?
actor_notes: Ilse genuinely believes this is about student honesty and enforcement; she has only seen the total number of cases and does not know the breakdown by course unit (that is in the data, not in her head).
She chaired the art. 41bis change and is visibly embarrassed when asked what the rules already allow; she won't raise it herself.
She resists 'train all 600' and 'it's a policy problem'; she warms up when the player shows the concentration and the appeal evidence, and asks for something targeted and doable before February.
She values nuance: players who say 'just trust the students' lose trust, as do players who treat students or part-timers as cheaters or incompetents.
Low risk appetite: a targeted pilot with the pioneers, using rules that already exist, is far easier for her to sell than anything that needs committees.
flavour_lines: We wrote a beautiful article 41bis. It has been used nine times. I've had more fire drills.
The detection software is 98% accurate, according to the detection software's brochure.
